findings.title: Metric depends on an event the plan does not define
findings.why_it_matters: A metric built on an event nobody tracks will read zero or stay empty, and the gap looks like a business result instead of a tracking hole.
findings.remediation: Define the event in events, or correct the name in the metric.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Metric depends on a deprecated event
findings.why_it_matters: A deprecated event stops arriving. A metric still reading it will decay toward zero and be mistaken for a real decline.
findings.remediation: Point the metric at the replacement event, then retire the old one.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Property name suggests personal data but is not marked pii
findings.why_it_matters: Personal data sent to analytics without a recorded decision is a privacy risk and a compliance question (data minimisation). The check is by name, so it can be wrong in both directions: it will miss a personal value with an innocent name.
findings.remediation: If the property holds personal data, set pii: true and record the lawful basis outside this plan, or stop sending it. If it does not, rename it so it is not mistaken for personal data.
references: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR): Art. 4(1) personal data; Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation.

findings.title: Same property name has different types on different events
findings.why_it_matters: A property that is a string on one event and a number on another cannot be stored in one warehouse column, so loads fail or silently coerce, and joins across events give wrong results.
findings.remediation: Give the property one type everywhere, or rename one of them if they mean different things.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Event cannot be tied to a user or device
findings.why_it_matters: An event that does not say who or which device produced it cannot be counted per user, joined to other events, or used in any retention or conversion metric.
findings.remediation: Add one of the identity_keys to the event as a required property, or set it once globally and list it on every event.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Metric depends on an event that is only planned
findings.why_it_matters: Until the event ships, the metric computes on partial or no data, and its history will have a break at the release date.
findings.remediation: Mark the metric as not ready until the event is active, or document the start date in the metric definition.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Event has no description or trigger
findings.why_it_matters: If nobody wrote down when the event fires, each analyst guesses, and the same event name ends up meaning different things in different dashboards.
findings.remediation: Add a description (what it means) and a trigger (the exact user or system action that emits it).
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Event has no owner
findings.why_it_matters: When an event breaks or its meaning must change, someone has to be asked. Without an owner the question has no answer, and broken events stay broken.
findings.remediation: Set the event's owner, or set a plan-level owner that covers every event.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Event name does not follow object_action
findings.why_it_matters: Names such as 'click' or 'CheckoutStarted' cannot be searched, grouped or governed consistently. A single convention is what lets a query select every event about one object, and keeps two spellings of one event from splitting its counts.
findings.remediation: Rename the event to object_action in snake_case, for example checkout_started. Deprecate the old name instead of reusing it.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Property name is not snake_case
findings.why_it_matters: Warehouses fold case differently, so 'planId' and 'plan_id' can become two columns or one, depending on the destination. A fixed style removes the ambiguity.
findings.remediation: Rename the property to snake_case, for example plan_id.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Enum property declares no allowed values
findings.why_it_matters: Without a closed list, every typo or new spelling becomes a new category, and a funnel split by that property silently loses rows.
findings.remediation: List every permitted value in allowed_values, or change the type to string.
references: Kohavi, Tang, Xu. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press, 2020 (chapter on instrumentation).

findings.title: Active event is used by no metric
findings.why_it_matters: An event nobody reads still costs volume, maintenance and privacy exposure. It is either missing from a metric that should use it, or not worth collecting.
findings.remediation: Connect the event to a metric, or deprecate it.
references: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR): Art. 4(1) personal data; Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation.
